body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Rating the quality of narrative comments on workplace-based assessment forms: development of a three-criterion checklist","authors":"Lindahl-Osei M, Fairbanks-Ruiz T, Chaudhry-Welsh A","year":2019,"venue":"Journal of Medical Education Research","doi":"10.5555/jmer.2019.0233","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We developed a checklist for rating written comments on workplace-based assessment forms. Three criteria were retained after two rounds of expert review: the comment names a specific observed behaviour, identifies a gap between performance and the expected standard, and proposes a concrete next step. Two trained raters applied the checklist to 600 comments from three internal medicine programmes. Agreement was substantial (kappa 0.74), and rating took about 40 seconds per comment. Only 35 percent of comments met all three criteria, and generic praise was the most common comment type. The checklist is intended for monitoring feedback quality, not for judging individual faculty."},{"title":"Prompted feedback fields on assessment forms and the specificity of written comments: a before-after study","authors":"Obuya-Hendricks S, Marchand-Iwata K","year":2022,"venue":"Assessment in Clinical Training","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"One residency programme replaced a single free-text box on its workplace-based assessment form with two prompts: one thing to keep doing and one thing to do differently. We rated 400 comments from the six months before and 400 from the six months after the change with a three-criterion checklist. The proportion of comments meeting all three criteria rose from 31 to 52 percent. Median comment length rose from 14 to 29 words, and the number of forms completed per month did not change. Raters were not blinded to the period, which may have inflated the difference."},{"title":"Brief faculty workshops on feedback and the quality of written comments: a controlled before-after study across two programmes","authors":"Kaczmarek-Bello J, Thorne-Adeyemi C, Vasquez-Lund R","year":2020,"venue":"Academic Medicine Teaching Reports","doi":"10.5555/amtr.2020.0418","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Faculty in one internal medicine programme attended two 20-minute workshops on written feedback, while a second programme continued as usual. Comments were rated blind to programme and period. At three months, the proportion of actionable comments rose by 14 percentage points in the workshop programme compared with 2 points in the comparison programme. By six months, without reminders, the difference had narrowed to 5 points. Attendance was 68 percent, and faculty who attended both sessions improved most. The authors conclude that brief teaching helps but fades without reinforcement."},{"title":"Resident perceptions of useful written feedback: a multi-site study of 540 trainees","authors":"Nakagawa-Pryce E, Oduro-Lambert F","year":2017,"venue":"Medical Education Quarterly","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We asked 540 residents in eight programmes to rate 30 real comments, stripped of identifiers, for usefulness. Comments that named a next step were rated most useful, and generic praise was rated least useful even when residents said they valued encouragement. Residents rated a comment's usefulness similarly whether it came from a senior or a junior faculty member. More than half said they rarely read the free-text comments on their forms because they expected them to be generic. The authors recommend that programmes monitor the specificity of comments rather than their number."},{"title":"Gendered language in narrative assessment comments for internal medicine residents","authors":"Abernathy-Mensah L, Rios-Kowalczyk D, Sorensen-Uba P","year":2021,"venue":"Medical Education Quarterly","doi":"10.5555/meq.2021.0907","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We analysed 3,100 narrative comments written for internal medicine residents in three programmes. Comments about women residents were more likely to describe personal attributes such as being pleasant or hardworking, and comments about men were more likely to describe clinical reasoning. After adjustment for postgraduate year and rotation, women were 1.4 times as likely as men to receive a comment with no actionable content. Differences were largest in comments written by faculty who completed the fewest forms. The authors recommend reporting feedback quality by resident gender whenever it is monitored."},{"title":"Monthly individual feedback reports to faculty on their assessment comments: a run-chart evaluation","authors":"Delacroix-Amoah B, Hughes-Nakamura T","year":2024,"venue":"Assessment in Clinical Training","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"A programme sent each faculty member a monthly one-page report showing a sample of their own written comments rated against a three-criterion checklist, with the programme median for comparison. Over 14 months, the monthly median proportion of actionable comments rose from 28 to 47 percent, with a shift on the run chart from month five. Faculty who opened the report email more than half the time improved most. The number of forms completed per resident did not fall. There was no comparison group, and a new assessment policy was introduced during month nine."},{"title":"Time from encounter to form completion and the specificity of written feedback","authors":"Wojcik-Addo H, Brennan-Sato M","year":2015,"venue":"Clinical Teacher Exchange","doi":"10.5555/cte.2015.0055","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We examined 1,800 workplace-based assessment forms and the delay between the observed encounter and the completion of the form. Comments on forms completed within 24 hours were more specific than those completed after 48 hours: 41 percent against 19 percent met all three quality criteria. Forms completed late were more often completed in batches at the end of a rotation. Programme size and rotation type did not explain the difference. The authors suggest that prompting completion soon after the encounter may improve comment quality more than lengthening the form."}]}
